Milk’s main protein, held as micelles that scatter light: 1 % milk powder in water (about 3.5 mg/mL casein) is cloudy white, and milk itself opaque. Proteases cut it into peptides, which do not scatter, so the milk clears (turbidity calibrated to that look).
What a protease leaves of a protein: short, soluble peptides (a casein gives about twenty).

A protease from the pancreas: cuts casein into soluble peptides, best near pH 8, and denatures above about 50 °C. Rate constants illustrative, calibrated so 1 % trypsin clears 1 % milk powder in a few minutes at 35 °C.

A pseudo-substance measured by mass (1 g/mol, so moles are grams). Cells of about 80 % water whose sap is about 0.45 osmol/kg, under turgor, so fresh tissue has a water potential near −0.75 MPa: isotonic with about 0.3 M sucrose (textbook range 0.25–0.35 M). Wall modulus and exchange time of the right order for 1 cm cylinders.

Measured by mass (1 g/mol). Its cells hold the red pigment betanin (about 0.15 mg/g) in their vacuoles behind two membranes; heat above about 50 °C or ethanol above about a quarter by volume destroys them, and the pigment leaks out.

identity.name: Baker’s yeast (dried, as its fermenting enzymes)

provenance.notes: A pseudo-substance: the fermenting capacity of dried yeast by mass (nominal 100 kDa per unit). Anaerobically it turns glucose and fructose into ethanol and carbon dioxide (two of each), sucrose (split by invertase) and maltose (by maltase, more slowly) into four of each, and cannot use lactose or starch. Respiring cells also pass electrons to methylene blue, decolourising it. Heat above about 45–50 °C kills it. Rates illustrative, calibrated so 1 % yeast with 0.1 M glucose gives about two millilitres of gas a minute at 35 °C.

references: Methylene blue λmax 664 nm, ε about 7.4 × 10⁴ M⁻¹ cm⁻¹; reduced (leuco) form colourless

identity.name: Pondweed (Elodea or Cabomba, as its photosynthesis)

provenance.notes: A pseudo-substance measured by fresh mass (nominal 1000 g/mol): a sprig’s photosynthesis. It fixes dissolved inorganic carbon (from hydrogencarbonate) and gives off oxygen, faster in brighter light up to saturation (half at about 300 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹), red light best, blue nearly as good, green poorly; its enzymes speed up with warmth and fail above about 35–40 °C. Calibrated so 5 g in 0.1 M hydrogencarbonate 10 cm from the lamp gives about 0.3–0.4 mL of oxygen a minute.

identity.name: Chloroplast suspension (isolated from spinach, as its light reactions)

provenance.notes: Isolated chloroplasts in light pass electrons from water to an artificial acceptor, DCPIP, which turns colourless (the Hill reaction); no light, no reaction; boiled, they do nothing. Kept cold they last a day or two; at room temperature they lose activity over hours. Rate calibrated so the blue goes in a few minutes 20 cm from a lamp.
The main photosynthetic pigment: blue-green, bands at 430 and 662 nm; on silica in 9:1 hexane–propanone it runs at Rf about 0.55.
An accessory pigment: yellow-green, bands at 453 and 642 nm; more polar than chlorophyll a, so it runs lower (Rf about 0.45).
An orange carotenoid with no polar groups: it runs almost with the solvent front (Rf about 0.95).
A yellow carotenoid with hydroxyl groups: more polar than carotene, Rf about 0.65.
Chlorophyll a that has lost its magnesium (in old or acidified extracts): olive-grey, Rf about 0.8.

identity.name: Leafy shoot (privet or laurel, cut under water)

provenance.notes: A pseudo-substance: 1 g of shoot carries about 30 cm² of leaf (one side). Its stomata open to a conductance of 0.3 mol m⁻² s⁻¹ in good light, half open at 50 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹, and a tenth open in the dark. A 5 g shoot 20 cm from a lamp in still air at 20 °C and 50 % humidity takes up about 0.02 mL a minute.

A pseudo-enzyme: the gross photosynthesis of the algae in pond water, oxygen from dissolved inorganic carbon. At 5 mg/L (as 1000 g/mol), 250 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹ and 21 °C in water with 2 mM hydrogencarbonate it gives off about 5.5 mg/L of oxygen a day. Algae concentrate carbon, so it saturates at low hydrogencarbonate (Km 0.5 mM).

A pseudo-enzyme: the aerobic respiration of everything living in pond water, using dissolved oxygen in light and dark alike and returning carbon dioxide. At 5 mg/L (as 1000 g/mol) and 21 °C it uses about 1.5 mg/L of oxygen a day; it slows only near anoxia (Km 3 µM).
A pseudo-substance: 1 g takes up about 0.25 µmol of oxygen a minute at 25 °C (0.37 mL an hour), doubling roughly every 9 °C (Q10 2.2), giving out as much carbon dioxide (RQ 1 for carbohydrate).
The control: seeds killed by boiling, and rinsed in disinfectant so that microbes on them do not respire either.
